3.6  Completeness

Soundness (Theorem 3.5.2) says that the rules of Chapters 1 and 2 never lead from true premises to a false conclusion: whatever can be derived is true in every row where the premises are. That answers half of the chapter’s question. The other half is the converse. Could the rules be too weak, so that some sequent is true in every row and yet no derivation of it exists? This section proves that they are not: every truth-table consequence has a derivation. The proof reads a derivation off the truth table, one row at a time, and then glues the rows together with excluded middle.

3.6.1. The question soundness leaves open

Recall the two relations from Section 3.4. Γ⊢ψ says that there is a derivation of ψ from premises in Γ (Definition 1.2.3). Γ⊨ψ says that every valuation making all of Γ true makes ψ true (Definition 3.4.3). Soundness is the implication Γ⊢ψ ⇒ Γ⊨ψ. Its converse is not automatic. The rules are a list that people wrote down, and a list can leave something out. Suppose, as a thought experiment, that we struck RAA (Definition 2.5.1) from the list. Every derivation that remains is still a derivation, so soundness still holds. But the tautology p∨¬p would then have no derivation (this is the optional Theorem 3.5.4 of Section 3.5). So a sound list of rules can be too short. The question is whether our list is long enough.

Here is a sequent to keep in mind. The formula (p→q)∨(q→p) is a tautology: if q is true then p→q is true, and if q is false then q→p is true. Chapter 2 found a derivation of it (Exercise (C2: A disjunction from nothing)), but only after reaching for LEM, and nothing in Chapter 2 promised that a derivation would be there to find. We want a theorem that promises it in advance, for every tautology and every valid sequent.

We are going to prove:

If Γ is a list of formulas and Γ⊨ψ, then Γ⊢ψ.

The plan has two ideas, one per row and one for all the rows together.

  1. One row gives one derivation. Fix a row of the truth table, that is, a valuation v. Write each atom as it stands in that row: p if v makes p true, ¬p if v makes it false. From these signed atoms we will derive the formula ψ if ψ is true in the row, and ¬ψ if it is false. The derivation climbs the parse tree of ψ, one connective at a time.
  2. The rows are glued by excluded middle. If Γ⊨ψ, the first idea gives ψ from Γ and the signed atoms of each row. Two rows that differ only at the atom p have derivations from “…,p” and from “…,¬p”. The rule ∨E applied to p∨¬p merges them into one derivation that no longer mentions p. Removing the atoms one at a time leaves a derivation from Γ alone.

The first idea is known as Kalmár’s lemma, and gluing rows by excluded middle is the standard way to finish; the route is the classical one. We keep the premises Γ throughout, and we isolate the two ingredients as lemmas so that each can be checked on its own. Before either, we need a little bookkeeping about derivations.

3.6.2. Bookkeeping: adding premises and chaining derivations

In Chapter 2 we learned to use a proved sequent as a single line (Definition 2.3.1): its derivation could be pasted in, with its letters replaced by formulas. The completeness proof uses this move dozens of times, so we now state exactly what it gives and check that pasting really produces a derivation.

Lemma 3.6.1 (Weakening and Cut)

Let Γ and Δ be lists of formulas, and let φ, ψ, α1,…,αm (m≥1), and β be formulas.

  • (a) Weakening. If Γ⊢ψ and every member of Γ is a member of Δ, then Δ⊢ψ. In particular, Γ⊢ψ implies Γ,φ⊢ψ.
  • (b) Cut. If Γ⊢φ and Γ,φ⊢ψ, then Γ⊢ψ.
  • (c) Chaining. If Γ⊢αi for every i=1,…,m, and α1,…,αm⊢β, then Γ⊢β.

In words: (a) extra premises never hurt; (b) a formula that has been derived may be used as a premise; (c) a sequent already proved can be applied to formulas already derived. Part (c) is Definition 2.3.1 for sequents: applying a proved sequent to formulas already derived, outside every box. Inside a box, Section 2.3’s expansion does the same job.

Idea. Part (a) is read off Definition 1.2.3, which asks only that the premises of the derivation belong to the list. For (b) and (c), write the derivations one after another and let the last one cite, instead of its premise αi, the last line of the derivation of αi. The only thing to check is the scope rule of Definition 1.4.2: the last line of a derivation lies in no box, so it stays available to everything written after it.

Proof. (a) A derivation witnessing Γ⊢ψ has premises that belong to Γ, hence to Δ, and its last line is ψ. By Definition 1.2.3 it witnesses Δ⊢ψ. The second sentence is the case where Δ is Γ,φ.

For (b) and (c) we prove one statement that contains both:

(∗) If Γ⊢αi for every i=1,…,m, and Γ,α1,…,αm⊢β, then Γ⊢β.

Part (b) is (∗) with m=1, α1=φ and β=ψ. Part (c) follows from (∗), since α1,…,αm⊢β gives Γ,α1,…,αm⊢β by (a).

To prove (∗), let Di be a derivation of αi with premises in Γ, for each i, and let E be a derivation of β with premises in Γ,α1,…,αm. If the last line of E is one of its premises, then β is a member of Γ, and the one-line derivation whose only line is the premise β shows Γ⊢β; or β is some αi, and Di shows Γ⊢β. Otherwise, build a list of lines F as follows.

  1. First, as premises, every premise of D1,…,Dm, and every premise of E that is a member of Γ.
  2. Then the lines of D1 that are not premises, then those of D2, and so on up to Dm, each with its boxes.
  3. Then the lines of E that are not premises, with its boxes.

Renumber the lines, and change each citation as follows. A citation of a premise that is in Γ now cites the premise line of step 1 carrying that formula. A citation in E of a premise αi that is not in Γ now cites the last line of Di; that line is not a premise of Di, because the premises of Di are in Γ and αi is not, so it was copied in step 2. Every other citation follows its line to its new number.

We check that F is a derivation (Definition 1.4.2). The premises come first and lie in no box. The boxes are those of the Di and of E, moved as blocks, so two boxes are still disjoint or nested, each still begins with its assumption, and each line lies in exactly the boxes it lay in before. Hence a line and a box that were available at a citing line are still available there, since the boxes containing each are unchanged. A premise line of step 1 lies in no box and comes first, so it is available at every later line. The last line of Di lies in no box (it was the last line of a derivation) and comes before every line of E, so it is available at every line of E. Each line carries the same formula and the same justification as before, citing lines with the same formulas, so it is an instance of the same rule. Finally, the last line of F is the last line of E, namely β, and it lies in no box. The premises of F are all in Γ. Therefore Γ⊢β, which proves (∗).

The lemma is pure bookkeeping, but it is what makes “cite a proved sequent as one line” honest. From now on, when a derivation cites a sequent proved earlier as a single line, the lemma (for a line in no box) or Definition 2.3.1 (for a line inside a box, where the cited lines are repeated inside the box first) is the reason the result is a derivation in the primitive rules. As Section 3.5 said, soundness was proved for the primitive rules, and a line citing a derived rule abbreviates a pasted derivation; for whole derivations, part (c) is the precise form of “abbreviates”, and inside a box the pasting of Definition 2.3.1 is the same bookkeeping.

Quick check. Suppose Γ⊢α and Γ⊢¬α. Which part of Lemma 3.6.1, applied to which proved sequent, gives Γ⊢χ for every formula χ?

Solution. Part (c) with m=2, α1=α, α2=¬α and β=χ, applied to Proposition 2.1.1, P,¬P⊢Q, with α for P and χ for Q.

3.6.3. The rules prove their own truth tables

Each line of the truth table of a connective says something like “with α true and β false, α→β comes out false”. Read with signs, that line is a sequent: from α and ¬β, conclude ¬(α→β). If every such sequent is derivable, then the rules know the truth tables. This is the key to the first idea of the plan. Section 3.3 began by reading the tables off the rules; the lemma below makes that reading exact: every line of every table is a derivable sequent.

Lemma 3.6.2 (The Rules Prove the Truth Tables)

For all formulas α and β, the following sequents are derivable, by derivations that do not use RAA.

  • (i) (¬1) α⊢¬¬α, and (⊥1) ⊢¬⊥.
  • (ii) (∧1) α,β⊢α∧β; (∧2) ¬α⊢¬(α∧β); (∧3) ¬β⊢¬(α∧β).
  • (iii) (∨1) α⊢α∨β; (∨2) β⊢α∨β; (∨3) ¬α,¬β⊢¬(α∨β).
  • (iv) (→1) ¬α⊢α→β; (→2) β⊢α→β; (→3) α,¬β⊢¬(α→β).
  • (v) (↔1) α,β⊢α↔β; (↔2) ¬α,¬β⊢α↔β; (↔3) α,¬β⊢¬(α↔β); (↔4) ¬α,β⊢¬(α↔β).

Each sequent has as premises only the parts it needs, each as itself or negated. For instance, α∧β is false as soon as α is false, whatever β is, and (∧2) has the single premise ¬α. This economy will matter: when the proof of the next lemma uses a row, it needs to know something only about the parts the row mentions.

Idea. Most of the sequents are already in the book: rules of Chapter 1, or results of Chapter 2 with α and β put in for the letters. The others are short derivations of the kinds Chapter 2 practiced: a box that repeats a premise, or a ¬I box that reaches a clash. The only thing to watch is that no step, and no cited result, uses RAA.

Proof. The table lists, for each sequent, the rows of the truth table it covers (by Definition 3.3.2) and where its derivation comes from. The letters of the Chapter 2 results are replaced by α and β, as Definition 2.3.1 allows.

Nor do the cited results: Proposition 2.1.2 and Example (Two negations from one premise) come from Sections 2.1 and 2.2, before RAA was introduced, and Chapter 2 derived De Morgan’s laws (b) and (c) without it (it says so right after the derivations of Proposition 2.5.5). The ¬ connective needs only one sequent. When α is false, ¬α is true, and the “sequent” ¬α⊢¬α is a one-line derivation; only the other row, (¬1), needs a proof.

Warning. The sequents of Lemma 3.6.2 go from the parts to the whole. Read backwards they are false. For instance α∨β⊢α is not derivable in general: the row p=F, q=T makes p∨q true and p false, so p∨q⊬p by Corollary 3.5.3. A row of a table tells us the value of the whole from the values of the parts, never the other way round.

3.6.4. One row, one derivation

We now name the formulas that “write down a row”.

A signed formula is a formula as it stands in one row: itself if the row makes it true, its negation if the row makes it false.

For a valuation v and a formula φ, the signed formula φv is φv:={φif v(φ)=T,¬φif v(φ)=F. In particular, for an atom p, the signed atom pv is p or ¬p. For example, if v(p)=T and v(q)=F, then pv=p, qv=¬q, (p→q)v=¬(p→q) and (q→p)v=q→p. Whatever v is, v(φv)=T: the signed formula is always the true one of φ and ¬φ, by the clause for ¬ in Definition 3.3.2.

The signed atoms p1v,…,pnv describe the row of v completely, as far as p1,…,pn go. The next lemma says they are enough premises to derive the signed version of any formula built from these atoms.

Lemma 3.6.3 (One Row of the Truth Table Is Derivable)

Let φ be a formula, let p1,…,pn (n≥0) be atoms among which are all the atoms of φ, and let v be a valuation. Then p1v,…,pnv⊢φv.

In words: in each row of the truth table of φ, the value of φ can be derived from the values of its atoms, where “value T” is written as the formula and “value F” as its negation.

Idea. Climb the parse tree. At an atom, φv is one of the premises. At a connective, the induction hypothesis gives the signed parts αv, βv, and Lemma 3.6.2 has a sequent from exactly those signed parts to the signed whole. So structural induction (Theorem 3.2.3), with Lemma 3.6.1 (c) to chain, does the whole job. The only care is to pick, for each pair of values, the row whose premises are the signs we actually have.

Proof. Fix the atoms p1,…,pn and the valuation v, and write Σ for the list p1v,…,pnv. We prove, by structural induction (Theorem 3.2.3), that every formula φ has the property

if every atom of φ is among p1,…,pn, then Σ⊢φv.

Every atom of an immediate part α or β of a formula is an atom of the formula itself, so when φ satisfies the “if”, so do its immediate parts, and the induction hypothesis applies to them.

Atoms. Let φ be an atom among p1,…,pn, say φ=pi. Then φv=piv is a member of Σ, and the one-line derivation whose only line is the premise piv shows Σ⊢φv.

The formula ⊥. By Definition 3.3.2, v(⊥)=F, so ⊥v=¬⊥. By (⊥1) of Lemma 3.6.2, ⊢¬⊥, and weakening (Lemma 3.6.1 (a)) gives Σ⊢¬⊥.

Negation. Let φ=¬α, and assume Σ⊢αv.

  • Case v(α)=T. Then αv=α, and v(¬α)=F, so φv=¬¬α. From Σ⊢α and (¬1), α⊢¬¬α, chaining (Lemma 3.6.1 (c)) gives Σ⊢¬¬α.
  • Case v(α)=F. Then αv=¬α, and v(¬α)=T, so φv=¬α=αv. The hypothesis is already the claim.

Conjunction. Let φ=α∧β, and assume Σ⊢αv and Σ⊢βv. By Definition 3.3.2, v(α∧β)=T exactly when v(α)=v(β)=T.

  • Case v(α)=v(β)=T. Then φv=α∧β, αv=α, βv=β. Chaining Σ⊢α and Σ⊢β with (∧1), α,β⊢α∧β, gives Σ⊢α∧β.
  • Case v(α)=F. Then φv=¬(α∧β) and αv=¬α. Chaining Σ⊢¬α with (∧2), ¬α⊢¬(α∧β), gives Σ⊢¬(α∧β). The hypothesis for β is not used.
  • Case v(α)=T, v(β)=F. Then φv=¬(α∧β) and βv=¬β, and chaining Σ⊢¬β with (∧3) gives Σ⊢¬(α∧β).

Implication. Let φ=α→β, and assume Σ⊢αv and Σ⊢βv. By Definition 3.3.2, v(α→β)=F exactly when v(α)=T and v(β)=F.

  • Case v(α)=F. Then φv=α→β and αv=¬α. Chaining Σ⊢¬α with (→1), ¬α⊢α→β, gives Σ⊢α→β.
  • Case v(α)=T, v(β)=T. Then φv=α→β and βv=β. Chaining Σ⊢β with (→2), β⊢α→β, gives Σ⊢α→β.
  • Case v(α)=T, v(β)=F. Then φv=¬(α→β), αv=α and βv=¬β. Chaining Σ⊢α and Σ⊢¬β with (→3), α,¬β⊢¬(α→β), gives Σ⊢¬(α→β).

Disjunction and biconditional. These go as for implication. For each pair of values of α and β, the table in the proof of Lemma 3.6.2 names a sequent whose premises are among αv, βv and whose conclusion is φv: for ∨, (∨1) if v(α)=T, (∨2) if v(α)=F and v(β)=T, (∨3) if both are F; for ↔, (↔1) to (↔4) for the value pairs T T, F F, T F, F T. Chaining the induction hypotheses for those premises with that sequent gives Σ⊢φv.

The atoms and ⊥ have the property, and each formation clause preserves it, so by Theorem 3.2.3 every formula has it. This proves the lemma.

Each case used the induction hypothesis only for the parts named in the premises of its sequent: the conjunction case with α false never looked at β. That is the economy of Lemma 3.6.2 at work. The disjunction and biconditional cases are written out in Exercise (C1: The remaining cases).

Here is the lemma run on one formula, with every chained sequent written as a line.

Example (Deriving one row)

Let φ=p→(q∧¬p) and let v(p)=v(q)=T. Find φv, and write the derivation of pv,qv⊢φv that the proof of Lemma 3.6.3 produces.

Solution. Compute up the parse tree: v(¬p)=F, so v(q∧¬p)=F, and since v(p)=T, v(φ)=F. So φv=¬(p→(q∧¬p)), and the premises are pv=p and qv=q.

The proof climbs the same tree. At ¬p with v(p)=T, it is the negation case with α true: (¬1) gives ¬¬p. At q∧¬p, the values are T and F: (∧3) gives ¬(q∧¬p) from (¬p)v=¬¬p. At the root, the values are T and F: (→3) gives the goal from p and ¬(q∧¬p). Written as a derivation, with each sequent of Lemma 3.6.2 cited as a derived rule:

1p
2q
3¬¬p(¬1) 1
4¬(q∧¬p)(∧3) 3
5¬(p→(q∧¬p))(→3) 1, 4

The premise q is never cited. It was used only in computing which case applies: the ∧ case with β=¬p false needs only β’s sign, not q’s. A derivation need not use every premise (Definition 1.2.3).

Quick check. Let φ=p→¬q and v(p)=v(q)=T. What sequent does Lemma 3.6.3 provide, and which sequent of Lemma 3.6.2 does the proof use at the root?

Solution. Here v(¬q)=F, so v(φ)=F, and the lemma gives p,q⊢¬(p→¬q). At the root the values are T and F, so the proof uses (→3), α,¬β⊢¬(α→β), with α=p and β=¬q. Its premise ¬β=¬¬q comes from the negation case below it: q⊢¬¬q, by (¬1).

3.6.5. Gluing the rows: splitting on an atom

Lemma 3.6.3 derives a formula from the signed atoms of one row. A sequent Γ⊢ψ mentions no row at all. The signed atoms must be removed, and the tool for that is excluded middle.

Lemma 3.6.4 (Splitting on an Atom)

Let Δ be a list of formulas, p an atom and ψ a formula. If Δ,p⊢ψ and Δ,¬p⊢ψ, then Δ⊢ψ.

Idea. This is proof by cases on p∨¬p. Proposition 2.5.3 gives p∨¬p with no premises, and ∨E (Definition 1.6.1) needs a box that reaches ψ from p and a box that reaches ψ from ¬p. The two given derivations are exactly the contents of those boxes, once their premise p (or ¬p) is replaced by the box’s assumption.

Before reading on: this is the only place in the completeness proof where a classical rule enters. Where exactly, and why could the ¬I of Chapter 2 not do the job?

Proof. Let D be a derivation of ψ with premises in Δ,p, and E one with premises in Δ,¬p. Build a list of lines as follows.

  1. As premises, every premise of D or of E that is a member of Δ.
  2. The line p∨¬p, justified by Proposition 2.5.3 (LEM) with p for P; it cites nothing.
  3. A box that opens with the assumption p, followed by the lines of D that are not premises, with their boxes. A citation of a premise of D that is in Δ now cites the premise line of step 1; a citation of the premise p now cites the assumption. If the last line of D is itself a premise, the box is shorter: if that premise is p, the box is the assumption alone, which is then its last line; otherwise the box is the assumption followed by ψ, by R, citing the premise line carrying ψ.
  4. A second box, built from E in the same way, opening with the assumption ¬p.
  5. The line ψ, by ∨E, citing line 2 of this list and the two boxes.

This is a derivation (Definition 1.4.2). The premises lie in no box and come first, so they are available everywhere. Inside the first box, the lines of D keep their boxes, which now sit inside the new box, and they cite the same lines and boxes as before, or a premise line, or the assumption, which is available at every line of its own box. As in the proof of Lemma 3.6.1, each line is still an instance of its rule. The last line of the first box is ψ, and it is a line of that box itself and not of a box inside it: it was the last line of D, which lies in no box of D (or it is the assumption itself, or the repetition line). The same holds for the second box. Both boxes and the line p∨¬p lie in no box, and neither does the last line, so they are available at it. Hence the last line is an instance of ∨E, and the list is a derivation of ψ whose premises are all in Δ. So Δ⊢ψ.

kψ∨E i, a–b, c–d

The answer to the prompt: the classical rule enters at line i. Proposition 2.5.3 was derived in Chapter 2 with RAA, and nothing else in the proof of this lemma is classical. ¬I could not replace it: ¬I produces a negation, and here we need a disjunction with no premises to split on. Nothing in the proof uses that p is an atom; the lemma holds for any formula in place of p, but atoms are all we shall split on.

3.6.6. The completeness theorem

Now the plan of the opening can be carried out.

Theorem 3.6.5 (Completeness)

Let Γ be a list of formulas and ψ a formula. If Γ⊨ψ, then Γ⊢ψ.

A list is finite, as in Definition 1.2.3. That matters: the proof works with the atoms that occur in Γ and ψ, and it needs them to be finitely many.

Idea. Step roadmap. ① List the atoms p1,…,pn of Γ and ψ. ② Claim: for every valuation v, Γ,p1v,…,pnv⊢ψ. If v makes all of Γ true, then ψ is true in that row, and Lemma 3.6.3 derives it. If v makes some premise γ false, the lemma derives ¬γ, which clashes with the premise γ. ③ Remove the signed atoms, last first, by Lemma 3.6.4. To remove pj we need derivations from both pj and ¬pj with the same other signed atoms: two rows that differ only at pj. That is why the Claim must hold for every valuation, not just one.

Proof. Step 1. The list Γ is finite and each formula has finitely many symbols, so only finitely many atoms occur in Γ or ψ. List them without repetition as p1,…,pn, where n≥0.

Step 2.

Claim. For every valuation v,  Γ,p1v,…,pnv⊢ψ.

Proof of Claim. Let v be a valuation, and write Σ for p1v,…,pnv.

Case 1: v(γ)=T for every member γ of Γ. Since Γ⊨ψ, by Definition 3.4.3 v(ψ)=T, so ψv=ψ. Every atom of ψ is among p1,…,pn, so Lemma 3.6.3 gives Σ⊢ψ, and weakening (Lemma 3.6.1 (a)) gives Γ,Σ⊢ψ.

Case 2: v(γ)=F for some member γ of Γ. Then γv=¬γ. Every atom of γ is among p1,…,pn, so Lemma 3.6.3 gives Σ⊢¬γ, and by weakening Γ,Σ⊢¬γ. Also Γ,Σ⊢γ, by the one-line derivation whose only line is the premise γ. By Proposition 2.1.1, γ,¬γ⊢ψ. Chaining (Lemma 3.6.1 (c)) gives Γ,Σ⊢ψ.

Step 3. For each integer j with 0≤j≤n, let S(j) be the statement for every valuation v,Γ,p1v,…,pjv⊢ψ, where for j=0 the list of signed atoms is empty. The Claim is S(n).

Claim. If 1≤j≤n and S(j) holds, then S(j−1) holds.

Proof of Claim. Let v be a valuation. Let v+ be the valuation that agrees with v at every atom except that v+(pj)=T, and v− the one that agrees with v except that v−(pj)=F; by Definition 3.3.1, a valuation may assign any value to each atom, so both exist. The atoms p1,…,pj−1 are different from pj, so v+ and v− agree with v on them, and piv+=piv−=piv for i<j. Also pjv+=pj and pjv−=¬pj. Applying S(j) to v+ and to v− gives, with Δ standing for the list Γ,p1v,…,pj−1v, Δ,pj⊢ψandΔ,¬pj⊢ψ. By Lemma 3.6.4, Δ⊢ψ. Since v was arbitrary, this is S(j−1).

It remains to go down from S(n) to S(0), which takes n applications of the Claim. We count the applications made: for m∈N, let T(m) say “if m≤n, then S(n−m) holds”. T(0) says that S(n) holds, which is Step 2. Suppose T(m) holds, and let m+1≤n. Then m≤n, so S(n−m) holds by T(m); and j:=n−m satisfies 1≤j≤n, because 0≤m≤n−1. The Claim gives S(j−1)=S(n−(m+1)), which is T(m+1). By Axiom 3.2.1, T(m) holds for every m∈N, and T(n) is S(0).

Step 4. S(0) says that Γ⊢ψ, for every valuation v; there is at least one valuation (for instance the one making every atom true), so Γ⊢ψ. This proves the theorem.

If n=0, the formulas of Γ and ψ are built from ⊥ alone, and Step 3 does nothing: S(0) is the Claim itself.

A common alternative route first turns Γ⊨ψ into a single tautology, ⊨γ1→(γ2→⋯→(γk→ψ)), proves completeness for tautologies, and then unpacks the implications with →E. Keeping Γ as premises, as Step 2 does, costs one extra case (a false premise) and saves that detour.

Let us run the proof on the tautology of the opening.

Example (The method on a tautology)

Run the proof of Theorem 3.6.5 on ⊨(p→q)∨(q→p), and write the derivation it produces, citing the sequents of Lemma 3.6.2 as derived rules.

Solution. Write χ for (p→q)∨(q→p). The list Γ is empty and the atoms are p1=p, p2=q. Every valuation makes χ true (if v(q)=T the left side is true; otherwise the right side is), so Step 2 is always Case 1, and Lemma 3.6.3 produces four short derivations, one per row:

  • p,q⊢χ: p→q by (→2) from q, then ∨I;
  • p,¬q⊢χ: q→p by (→1) from ¬q, then ∨I;
  • ¬p,q⊢χ and ¬p,¬q⊢χ: p→q by (→1) from ¬p, then ∨I.

(In the row p=F, q=T, both (→1) and (→2) would do; the proof of Lemma 3.6.3 uses (→1) whenever α is false.) Step 3 first splits on q=p2, twice: once with p and once with ¬p among the premises. Then it splits on p=p1, once. Three uses of Lemma 3.6.4 in two rounds. Pasting as in its proof, the last split is the outermost:

1p∨¬pLEM
2p
3q∨¬qLEM
4q
5p→q(→2) 4
6(p→q)∨(q→p)∨I 5
7¬q
8q→p(→1) 7
9(p→q)∨(q→p)∨I 8
10(p→q)∨(q→p)∨E 3, 4–6, 7–9
11¬p
12q∨¬qLEM
13q
14p→q(→1) 11
15(p→q)∨(q→p)∨I 14
16¬q
17p→q(→1) 11
18(p→q)∨(q→p)∨I 17
19(p→q)∨(q→p)∨E 12, 13–15, 16–18
20(p→q)∨(q→p)∨E 1, 2–10, 11–19

The derivation has 20 lines. The one found by search in Exercise (C2: A disjunction from nothing) has 13, and splits only once. Here the split on q inside the box of ¬p (lines 12–19) is wasted: both of its boxes do the same thing, because in the rows with p false the value of q does not matter. The proof is a method that always works, not a recipe for short derivations; to find a short one, search as in Section 2.6.

Warning. Completeness promises a derivation, not a short one. For a sequent with n atoms, the proof builds 2n row derivations and glues them with 2n−1 splittings: with n=10 atoms, that is 1024 row derivations and 1023 uses of LEM. The theorem answers “is there a derivation?”, not “how short is the shortest?”.

With soundness, completeness closes the circle.

Corollary 3.6.6 (Derivable Means Valid)

For every list of formulas Γ and every formula ψ, Γ⊢ψ⟺Γ⊨ψ. In particular, whether Γ⊢ψ holds can be decided by checking the 2n rows of a truth table, where n is the number of atoms occurring in Γ and ψ.

Proof. (⇒) is Theorem 3.5.2 and (⇐) is Theorem 3.6.5. For the second sentence, let p1,…,pn be the atoms occurring in Γ and ψ. By Lemma 3.3.1, the values of the members of Γ and of ψ under a valuation depend only on its values at p1,…,pn, so Γ⊨ψ holds exactly when it holds in each of the 2n rows of the joint truth table. That is a finite check, and by the first sentence it decides Γ⊢ψ.

So a question that looks as if it needs a search through infinitely many possible derivations can be settled by a finite table. The search for a derivation may still be the quicker way to a yes, and one row is the quickest way to a no (Corollary 3.5.3), but neither is needed.

Remark. We defined Γ⊢ψ only for a list, that is, for finitely many premises. One may allow an infinite collection Γ of premises and say Γ⊢ψ when ψ is derivable from finitely many members of Γ (a derivation has finitely many lines, so it can only use finitely many). The equivalence with Γ⊨ψ still holds for infinite Γ; this is the compactness theorem of propositional logic. We do not prove it, and nothing in the book depends on it. Our proof does not reach it: Step 1 needs finitely many atoms.

3.6.7. Two roads to every answer

We now have two independent ways to settle any question “is Γ⊢ψ?”. One is to search for a derivation, as in Section 2.6. The other is to check a table, and Corollary 3.6.6 says the two always agree. Here are two of Chapter 2’s classical laws settled by the table first.

De Morgan’s law (d). Is ¬(p∧q)⊨¬p∨¬q? The four rows: pq¬(p∧q)¬p∨¬qTTFFTFTTFTTTFFTT In every row where the premise is T, so is the conclusion. So ¬(p∧q)⊨¬p∨¬q, and by Theorem 3.6.5, ¬(p∧q)⊢¬p∨¬q.

Peirce’s law. Is (p→q)→p⊨p? Work backwards from F (Section 3.3). A refuting row would need p false. Then p→q is true, so (p→q)→p is “true implies false”, which is false. So no row makes the premise true and the conclusion false: (p→q)→p⊨p, and by Theorem 3.6.5, (p→q)→p⊢p.

Both answers came before anyone found a derivation. Chapter 2 found both by hand (Proposition 2.5.5 (d), and Proposition 2.5.4, whose ⊢((P→Q)→P)→P gives the sequent by →E), and the derivations there use RAA. Completeness explains why a search had to succeed; it does not say how.

Section 3.4 remarked that the tables do not see which of Chapter 2’s laws needed RAA. Now we can say why they cannot. A table decides Γ⊨ψ, and by Corollary 3.6.6 that is the same as derivability with all the rules, RAA included. A table has no column recording which rules a derivation uses. Whether a sequent can be derived without RAA is a question about a shorter list of rules, and for that list the completeness theorem is false, as the next paragraph explains. So no truth-table check can tell the laws that need RAA from those that do not.

Which rules did the proof of completeness itself use? Lemma 3.6.1 only pastes derivations. Lemma 3.6.2 uses no RAA, as its proof checks. Lemma 3.6.3 and the Claim chain those sequents, together with Proposition 2.1.1, which Chapter 2 derived before RAA appeared. The one classical step is the line p∨¬p of Lemma 3.6.4. So the theorem is really about the full list of rules, RAA included. Without RAA the list is sound but not complete, as the optional Theorem 3.5.4 shows for ⊢p∨¬p and ¬¬p⊢p; the proof above breaks exactly at the splitting.

Warning. Completeness does not say that a tautology has a derivation without RAA. It says there is a derivation from the rules of Chapters 1 and 2, all of them. The formula (p→q)∨(q→p) is a tautology, and every derivation found for it so far uses LEM or RAA. Whether a particular tautology can do without them is a different question, and a table cannot answer it.

3.6.8. Exercises

A. Check your understanding

Exercise (A1)

These questions are about Lemma 3.6.3 and Theorem 3.6.5.

  • (a) In the conjunction case of the proof of Lemma 3.6.3, suppose v(α)=F and v(β)=T. Which sequent of Lemma 3.6.2 is used, and which induction hypotheses?
  • (b) Where is RAA used in the proof of Theorem 3.6.5, including inside the results it cites?
  • (c) State the idea of the proof of Theorem 3.6.5 in two sentences.
  • (d) Run Step 2 of the proof for Γ=p, ψ=p∨q and the valuation with v(p)=F, v(q)=T: which case applies, and which sequent does it prove?
  • (e) Step 1 lists the atoms without repetition. Where in the proof is that used?
  • (f) Which step of the proof fails if Γ is allowed to be an infinite collection of formulas, each with its own atoms?

Solution. (a) (∧2), ¬α⊢¬(α∧β), and only the hypothesis for α, Σ⊢¬α. The hypothesis for β is not needed, because α∧β is false once α is.

(b) Only inside Lemma 3.6.4, at the line p∨¬p: Proposition 2.5.3 was derived with RAA. The sequents of Lemma 3.6.2 are derived without it, Lemma 3.6.1 only pastes derivations, and Proposition 2.1.1 comes before RAA in Chapter 2.

(c) Each row of the truth table gives a derivation of the conclusion from the premises and that row’s signed atoms: by Lemma 3.6.3 if the row makes every premise true, and from a clash with a false premise otherwise. Two rows that differ at one atom are merged by excluded middle and proof by cases, and after all the atoms are merged the signed atoms are gone.

(d) The valuation makes the premise p false, so Case 2 applies with γ=p. Lemma 3.6.3 gives ¬p,q⊢¬p (the atom case), the premise gives p, and Proposition 2.1.1 gives p∨q. The sequent proved is p,¬p,q⊢p∨q.

(e) In the Claim of Step 3: v+ and v− change only the value at pj, and they agree with v on p1,…,pj−1 only because those atoms differ from pj. If pj also appeared as some pi with i<j, then piv+=pj and piv−=¬pj would differ, and the two sequents would not share the list Δ that Lemma 3.6.4 needs.

(f) Step 1. Infinitely many atoms may occur, so there is no finite list p1,…,pn: the Claim would need infinitely many signed atoms as premises, which is not a list, and Step 3’s descent from S(n) has no n to start from.

Exercise (B3: Table first, then a derivation)

Decide by a truth table whether ¬(p↔q)⊨¬p↔q. If it holds, find a derivation of ¬(p↔q)⊢¬p↔q by search, where you may cite the sequents of Lemma 3.6.2 as derived rules. Which rule of your derivation is classical?

Solution. The table: pq¬(p↔q)¬p↔qTTFFTFTTFTTTFFFF The premise is true in rows 2 and 3, and so is the conclusion. So the entailment holds, and by Theorem 3.6.5 a derivation exists.

The search: the goal is a biconditional, so two boxes, one from ¬p to q and one from q to ¬p. In the second, the goal ¬p is a negation: a box on p, and p, q give p↔q by (↔1), which clashes with the premise. In the first, the goal q is an atom, the only premise is a negation, and nothing else applies: we are stuck, and assume ¬q. Then ¬p, ¬q give p↔q by (↔2), which clashes with the premise.

C. Going deeper

Exercise (C1: The remaining cases)

Write out in full the disjunction case and the biconditional case of the proof of Lemma 3.6.3, in the style of the implication case.

Solution. Throughout, Σ is p1v,…,pnv, and the induction hypotheses are Σ⊢αv and Σ⊢βv. “Chaining” is Lemma 3.6.1 (c).

Disjunction, φ=α∨β. By Definition 3.3.2, v(α∨β)=F exactly when v(α)=v(β)=F.

  • Case v(α)=T. Then φv=α∨β and αv=α. Chaining Σ⊢α with (∨1), α⊢α∨β, gives Σ⊢α∨β.
  • Case v(α)=F, v(β)=T. Then φv=α∨β and βv=β. Chaining Σ⊢β with (∨2) gives Σ⊢α∨β.
  • Case v(α)=v(β)=F. Then φv=¬(α∨β), αv=¬α and βv=¬β. Chaining both hypotheses with (∨3), ¬α,¬β⊢¬(α∨β), gives Σ⊢¬(α∨β).

Biconditional, φ=α↔β. By Definition 3.3.2, v(α↔β)=T exactly when v(α)=v(β). Each case uses both hypotheses.

  • Case T, T. φv=α↔β; chain Σ⊢α, Σ⊢β with (↔1).
  • Case F, F. φv=α↔β; chain Σ⊢¬α, Σ⊢¬β with (↔2).
  • Case T, F. φv=¬(α↔β); chain Σ⊢α, Σ⊢¬β with (↔3).
  • Case F, T. φv=¬(α↔β); chain Σ⊢¬α, Σ⊢β with (↔4).

The cases cover all four pairs of values, so in each the property holds for φ.

Marking scheme. (10 points)

  • 4: the ∨ case: the three value cases, each with the right sequent of Lemma 3.6.2 and only the hypotheses its premises need.
  • 4: the ↔ case: the four value cases, each with the right sequent and both hypotheses.
  • 1: names chaining (Lemma 3.6.1 (c)) as the step that combines the hypotheses with the sequent.
  • 1: says that the cases cover every pair of values.

Fatal errors (0 for the step): using a sequent whose premises are not the signed parts αv, βv of that case.

Exercise (C2: Exit check: completeness)

Close the section first, and write from memory.

  • (a) Prove Lemma 3.6.4: if Δ,p⊢ψ and Δ,¬p⊢ψ, then Δ⊢ψ.
  • (b) Prove Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 3.6.5 in full: from the Claim of Step 2, for every valuation v, Γ,p1v,…,pnv⊢ψ, deduce Γ⊢ψ. State the statement you prove by induction, and say which principle of induction you use.

Solution (Hint 1). For (a): excluded middle and proof by cases. For (b): remove the signed atoms from the end of the list, one at a time.

Solution (Hint 2). For (b): let S(j) say “for every valuation v, Γ,p1v,…,pjv⊢ψ”, and show that S(j) implies S(j−1) for 1≤j≤n.

Solution. (a) Let D derive ψ from premises in Δ,p, and E from premises in Δ,¬p. Write, as premises, those of D and E that lie in Δ; then p∨¬p by LEM (Proposition 2.5.3, a derived rule with no premises); then a box opening with p containing the nonpremise lines of D, in which citations of the premise p now cite the assumption and citations of premises in Δ cite the premise lines; then a box opening with ¬p, built from E in the same way; then ψ by ∨E, citing the line p∨¬p and the two boxes. (If D or E ends on a premise, its box is the assumption alone when that premise is the assumption’s formula, and otherwise the assumption followed by ψ by R.) Every copied line keeps its boxes, now inside the new box, and cites lines still available to it. The last line of each box is ψ, as a line of that box itself, because the last line of D or E lay in no box. The two boxes and the LEM line lie in no box, so they are available at the final line. So the result is a derivation of ψ from premises in Δ, and Δ⊢ψ.

(b) For 0≤j≤n, let S(j) be: for every valuation v, Γ,p1v,…,pjv⊢ψ. The Claim of Step 2 is S(n).

The step. Let 1≤j≤n and assume S(j). Let v be any valuation, and let v+, v− agree with v except that v+(pj)=T and v−(pj)=F. Since the pi are distinct, both agree with v on p1,…,pj−1. By S(j) for v+ and for v−, with Δ:=Γ,p1v,…,pj−1v: Δ,pj⊢ψ and Δ,¬pj⊢ψ. By (a), Δ⊢ψ. As v was arbitrary, S(j−1) holds.

The induction. We use Axiom 3.2.1 on m∈N with the statement T(m): “if m≤n, then S(n−m)”. T(0) is S(n). If T(m) holds and m+1≤n, then S(n−m) holds and j=n−m lies between 1 and n, so the step gives S(n−m−1), which is T(m+1). Hence T(n), which is S(0): for every valuation, Γ⊢ψ. Valuations exist, so Γ⊢ψ.

(Inducting downwards on j, or on the number of atoms removed, is the same argument; either earns full marks.)

Marking scheme. (10 points)

  • 3: (a) pastes both derivations into the two boxes of a ∨E on p∨¬p, with the premise p (or ¬p) redirected to the box’s assumption, and says why every citation is still available.
  • 1: (a) cites LEM (Proposition 2.5.3) as a derived rule.
  • 3: (b) sets up an induction on the number of atoms removed (or downward on j) with a statement quantified over every valuation, and names the induction principle.
  • 2: (b) in the step, applies the hypothesis to both valuations that differ at pj, and notes that they agree with v on the other atoms.
  • 1: (b) concludes Γ⊢ψ from S(0).

Fatal errors (0 for the step): splitting on an atom using the Claim for a single valuation only; an induction statement that fixes v before the induction, so that the two valuations of the step are not covered by the hypothesis.
